lines: Title: Newton's Inequalities on a Lattice

All real valued functions F that satisfisfy the Hadamard Fisher Inequalities  $F(\alpha\cap\beta)F(\alpha\cup\beta)\leq F(\alpha)F(\beta)$ for $\alpha,\beta\subseteq\left\{1,2,..,n\right\}$  also satisfy Newton's inequalities $(S^F_k)^2\geq S^F_{k-1} S^F_{k+1}$} for $1\leq k\leq n-1$ where $S^F_k=\frac{1}{(^n_k)} \sum_{\alpha\subseteq\left\{1,2,..n\right\},k=\left|\alpha\right|} F(\alpha)$ for $1\leq k\leq n$, $S^F_0=1$.

If A is a square matrix of order n and $\alpha\subseteq \left\{1,2,..n\right\}$ then $A[\alpha]$ will denote the sub matrix of A contained in the intersection of the rows and columns indexed by $\alpha$. Newton's inequalities have been shown to hold for Hermitian and M Matrices \cite[Theorem 1]{OH}. If A is either a non-negative definite Hermitian matrix  or a M Matrix and $\beta\subseteq\left\{1,2,..n\right\}$then the determinant   of A satisfies:

$\det A[\alpha] \det A[\beta] \geq \det A[\alpha\cap\beta]\det A[\alpha\cup\beta]$. If F is a real valued function then for $1\leq k \leq n$ define $S^F_k=\frac{1}{(^n_k)} \sum_{\alpha\subseteq\left\{1,2,..n\right\},k=\left|\alpha\right|} F(\alpha)$. We will show that if F satisfies $F(\alpha\cap\beta)F(\alpha\cup\beta)\leq F(\alpha)F(\beta)$ for all $\alpha$ and $\beta$ that are subsets of $\left\{1,2,..n\right\}$ with  $F(\phi)=1$ then $(S^F_k)^2\geq S^F_{k-1} S^F_{k+1}$.
Let n be a non negative integer. Let $<n>$ denote a set with n entries. and $\phi$ denote the empty set. For $\alpha\subseteq <n>$ let $\left|\alpha\right|$ denote the number of elements in $\alpha$

Define a total ordering on the elements of $<n>$. For $1\leq  k\leq n$ let $Q_{k,<n>}$ denote the set of strictly increasing sequences of length k whose entries are chosen from $<n>$. Note that $Q_{k,<n>}$ has  $(^n_k)$ entries.

The following lemma is similar to an identity established in \cite[Lemma 2]{OH} and will be used in the proof of the main result. In the proof of this lemma we view a matrix as a mapping from the Cartesian product of two finite sets into a set.
If F is a complex valued function with domain $Q_{k,<n>}$ then for $1\leq  k < n$

Let n be a non-negative integer and $1\leq  k< n$. Let H be the $Q_{k,<n>}\times Q_{k,<n>}$ matrix, $H(\alpha,\beta)=\frac{k-\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}{k+1-\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}$. Then all the elements on the diagonal of H equal 0. If we sum the elements in a row indexed by $\alpha$ we get

$\sum_{\beta\in Q_{k,<n>}}\frac{k-\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}{k+1-\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}$. We now reorder the sum  based on the number of elements in the intersection of the row index with the column index.  If the row index contains k elements then there are $(^k_i)$ ways to select i elements out of the row index. Since only these i elements can also be in the column index we have to remove all k of the elements in the row index from $<n>$ and  select the remaining k-i elements from a set of size n-k.  Thus for $0\leq i < k$ the number of terms in a row such that i of its elements are in the intersection of the column index  equals $(^{n-k}_{k-i})(^k_i)$. Hence $\sum_{\beta\in Q_{k,<n>}}H_{\alpha,\beta}=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\frac{k-i}{ k+1-i}(^{n-k}_{k-i})(^k_i)$.We apply Vandermonde's  identity in the form $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} (^{k+1}_i)(^{n-k-1}_{k-i-1})=(^n_{k-1})$ \cite {RA}. We observe that $\frac{(^n_{k+1})}{(^n_k)}=\frac{n-k}{k+1}$ and hence $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\frac{k-i}{ k+1-i}(^{n-k}_{k-i})(^k_i)=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\frac{(^{n-k-1}_{k-i-1})(^{k+1}_i)(^n_{k+1})}{(^n_k)}=\frac{(^n_{k+1})(^n_{k-1})}{(^n_k)}$.

Thus  all the row sums of H equal $\frac{(^n_{k+1})(^n_{k-1})}{(^n_k)}$.  Define the matrix S by $(s_{\alpha,\beta})=\frac{(^n_k)h_{\alpha,\beta}}{(^n_{k+1})(^n_{k-1})}$ for all $\alpha,\beta\in Q_{k,<n>}$. Then S is a symmetric non negative stochastic matrix with zeros on the diagonal. Since S is  non negative and stochastic with zeros on the diagonal each row and column of S has at least one element that is greater then or equal to $\frac{1}{(^n_k)}$. Since $s_{\alpha,\beta}=\frac{(^n_k)h_{\alpha,\beta}}{(^n_{k+1})(^n_{k-1})}\geq\frac{1}{(^n_k)} \Leftrightarrow\frac{(^n_k)}{(^n_{k+1})(^n_{k-1})}\frac{k-\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}{k+1-\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}\geq\frac{1}{(^n_k)}$ and $\frac{(^n_{k+1})(^n_{k-1})}{(^n_k)(^n_k)}=\frac{k}{k+1}\frac{n-k}{n-k+1}$ we have that  $s_{\alpha,\beta}\geq\frac{1}{(^n_k)}\Leftrightarrow\frac{k-\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}{k+1-\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}\geq\frac{k}{k+1}\frac{n-k}{n-k+1}$ and that $s_{\alpha,\beta}=\frac{1}{(^n_k)}\Leftrightarrow\frac{k-\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}{k+1-\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}=\frac{k}{k+1}\frac{n-k}{n-k+1}$.\newline

We will now show that for every pair $\alpha\neq\beta\in Q_{k,<n>}$ there exists $\gamma_1,\gamma_2.. ,\gamma_t\in Q_{k,<n>}$ such that $s_{\gamma_i,\gamma_{i+1}}\geq \frac{1}{(^n_k)},1\leq i < t$ with $\gamma_1=\alpha$ and $\gamma_t=\beta$.

Clearly $n\geq 2k-\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|$. If $n=2k-\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|$ then $\alpha\cup\beta=<n>$ and we have that $\frac{k}{k+1}\frac{n-k}{n-k+1}=\frac{k}{k+1}\frac{k-\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}{k+1-\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}<\frac{k-\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}{k+1-\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}$ and hence $s_{\alpha,\beta}>\frac{1}{(^n_k)}$.

If $k\geq2$ and $2k\geq n>2k-\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|$ then there exists $\omega\in Q_{k,<n>}$ such that $\beta\setminus(\alpha\cap\beta)\subseteq\omega$ and $s_{\alpha,\omega}\geq\frac{1}{(^n_k)}$. If $\phi=\alpha\cap\beta$ then $s_{\alpha,\beta}>\frac{1}{(^n_k)}$ otherwise there  exists $j\notin\alpha\cup\beta$ with $j\in\omega$ and $i\in\alpha\cap\beta$. Form $\gamma_1=(\alpha\setminus\left\{i\right\})\cup \left\{j\right\}$. Then $\left|\gamma_1\cap\beta\right|=\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|-1$ and $\gamma_1\in Q_{k,<n>}$. Also $\left|\gamma_1\cap\omega\right|=\left|\alpha\cap\omega\right|+1$. Since $n\leq 2k$ we have that $\frac{k}{k+1}\frac{n-k}{n-k+1}<\frac{k}{k+1}\frac{k}{k+1}<\frac{k-1}{k}\leq\frac{k-\left|\gamma_1\cap\omega\right|}{k-\left|\gamma_1\cap\omega\right|+1}$ and hence $s_{\omega,\gamma_1}\geq\frac{1}{(^n_k)}$.

Form $\omega_1=(\omega\setminus\left\{j\right\})\cup\left\{i\right\}$ then $\omega_1\in Q_{k,<n>}$ and since $\gamma_1\cap\omega_1= ((\alpha\setminus\left\{i\right\})\cup \left\{j\right\})\cap((\omega\setminus\left\{j\right\})\cup\left\{i\right\})=\alpha\cap\omega$ we have that $s_{\gamma_1,\omega_1}>\frac{1}{(^n_k)}$.

We repeat this procedure constructing $\gamma_2,\omega_2,....\gamma_{\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|},\omega_{\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}$ terminating in ${\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}$ steps when $\gamma_{\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}\cap\beta=\phi$ and $\omega_{\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}=\beta$.

If $n>2k$ then there exists $\tau\subseteq<n>$ such that $\phi=\tau\cap\beta=\tau\cap\alpha$,  $\left|\tau\right|>\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|$ and $\omega\in Q_{k,<n>}$ satisfying $\omega=(\beta\setminus(\alpha\cap\beta))\cup(\omega\cap\tau)$. Since $\alpha\cap\omega=\phi$ we have that  $s_{\alpha,\omega}\geq\frac{1}{(^n_k)}$. Since $\left|\tau\right|>\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|$ there exists $j\in \tau$, $j\notin\omega\cup\alpha\cup\beta$. Let $i\in\alpha\cap\beta$ and define $\gamma_1=(\alpha\setminus\left\{i\right\})\cup\left\{j\right\}$. Then $\gamma_1\in Q_{k,<n>}$ and $\gamma_1\cap\omega=\phi$. Thus  $s_{\omega,\gamma_1}\geq\frac{1}{(^n_k)}$. Furthermore $\left|\gamma_1\cap\beta\right|=\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|-1$. Select $p\in\tau\cap\omega$ and define $\omega_1=(\omega\setminus\left\{p\right\})\cup\left\{i\right\}$. Then $\omega_1\in Q_{k,<n>}$ and satisfies $\omega_1=(\beta\setminus(\gamma_1\cap\beta))\cup(\omega_1\cap\tau)$. Since $\gamma_1\cap\omega_1=\phi$ we have that  $s_{\gamma_1,\omega_1}\geq\frac{1}{(^n_k)}$. Define $\tau_1=\tau\setminus\left\{j\right\}$ then $\phi=\tau_1\cap\beta=\tau_1\cap\gamma_1$ and $\left|\tau_1\right|>\left|\gamma_1\cap\beta\right|$

We repeat this procedure constructing $\gamma_2,\omega_2,\tau_2....\gamma_{\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|},\omega_{\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|},\tau_{\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}$ terminating in ${\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}$ steps when $\gamma_{\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}\cap\beta=\phi$ and $\omega_{\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}=\beta$.
Thus in all cases there exists $\gamma_1,\gamma_2.. ,\gamma_t\in Q_{k,<n>}$ such that $s_{\gamma_i,\gamma_{i+1}}\geq \frac{1}{(^n_k)},1\leq i < t$ with $\gamma_1=\alpha$ and $\gamma_t=\beta$.

Since S is non negative and stochastic, for $ \epsilon>0,(\epsilon+1)I-S$ is a M matrix \cite {GF} and thus by continuity $I-S$ is a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix with 0 as a minimum eigenvalue. Let F be the $n\times n$ flat matrix i.e. $f_{i,j}=1$ for $1\leq i,j\leq n$.  For $0\leq t\leq 1$ define

$C(t)=(1-t)I+t\frac{1}{(^n_k)}F-S$. Zero is an eigenvalue of the matrix C(t)  and if $n\geq 2$ C(t) is irreducible for $0\leq t\leq 1$. Thus 0 is always a simple eigenvalue of C(t) for $0\leq t< 1$  \cite [see corollary 4.4 page 166] {ES}.  Thus all of the eigenvalues of C(t) must remain non-negative and hence $C(1)=\frac{1}{n}F-S$ is symmetric and non-negative definite. Thus

$\left|\frac{1}{(^n_k)}\sum_{\alpha\in Q_{k,<n>}} F(\alpha)\right|^2\geq\frac{1}{((^n_{k+1})(^n_{k-1})))}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\frac{k-i}{k+1-i}\sum_{\stackrel{k=\left|\alpha\subseteq<n>\right|}{k=\left|\beta\subseteq<n>\right|,i=\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}}F(\alpha)\overline{F(\beta)}$. Since this inequality has been shown to hold for all complex valued functions F it must also  holds for $\sqrt{-1}F$. Thus $\left|\frac{1}{(^n_k)}\sum_{\alpha\in Q_{k,<n>}} F(\alpha)\right|^2\geq$ \newline $\left|\frac{1}{((^n_{k+1})(^n_{k-1})))}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\frac{k-i}{k+1-i}\sum_{\stackrel{k=\left|\alpha\subseteq<n>\right|}{k=\left|\beta\subseteq<n>\right|,i=\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|}}F(\alpha)\overline{F(\beta)}\right|$.

Let F be a complex valued function on the subsets of $<n>$. For $0\leq k\leq n$ let $S^F_k$ denote the $k^{th}$ symmetric function on $<n>$ with respect to F. i.e. $S^F_k=\frac{1}{(^n_k)} {\sum_{\alpha\in Q_{k,<n>}} F(\alpha)}$.
Let F be a complex valued function on the subsets of $<n>$. Then define the functions:

$E_{k,i}^F$ equals the average  value of products $F(\alpha)\overline{F(\beta)}$ when $\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|=i$ and $k=\left|\alpha\right|=\left|\beta\right|$. $U_{k,i}^F$ equals the average  value of the products $F(\alpha)\overline{F(\beta)}$ when  $\left|\alpha\right|=k+1,\left|\beta\right|=k-1$ and $\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|=i$.
Let  F be a complex valued function defined on the subsets of $<n>$. Let k be $1\leq k< n$.
If for $0\leq i< k,  U_{k,i}^F$ is real and $E_{k,i}^F \geq U_{k,i}^F$
\newline Assume for $0\leq i< k, U_{k,i}^F$ is real and $E_{k,i}^F \geq U_{k,i}^F$   then
As a result of the definition of $E_{k,i}^F$ we have that

F is said to satisfy the \textsl{Hadamard-Fischer inequalities} on \newline $<n>$ if  F is a real valued function on the subsets of $<n>$ with $F(\phi)=1$ for all $\alpha\subseteq<n>$ and for all $\beta\subseteq<n> F(\alpha\cap\beta)F(\alpha\cup\beta)\leq F(\alpha)F(\beta)$.
The following are examples of functions that satisfy the Hadamard-Fischer inequalities:
\item Let $1\leq n$. Let $a_1,a_2,.....a_n$ be a sequence of non negative numbers. Then for all $\alpha\subseteq <n>$ define $F(\alpha)=\max_{i\in\alpha}a_i$.
\item Let $1\leq n$. Let $a_1,a_2,.....a_n$ be a sequence of non negative numbers. Then for all $\alpha\subseteq <n>$ define $F(\alpha)=\prod_{i\in\alpha}a_i$.
\item Let $1\leq n$. Let g be a sub additive function defined on on all the subsets of $<n>$ with $g(\phi)=0$. Let $x\geq1$.  Define $F(\alpha)= x^{g(\alpha)}$  for $\alpha\subseteq <n>$.
\item  Let $1\leq n$. Let A be a $n\times n$ M matrix. For all $\alpha\subseteq <n>$ define $F(\alpha)=\det A(\alpha)$ \cite {AO}.
\item Let $1\leq n$. Let A be a $n\times n$ totally positive matrix. For all $\alpha\subseteq <n>$ define $F(\alpha)=\det A(\alpha)$ \cite[page 85] {GK}.
\item Let $1\leq n$. Let A be a $n\times n$ positive definite Hermitian matrix. For all $\alpha\subseteq <n>$ define $F(\alpha)=\det A(\alpha)$.

A be a $n\times n$ matrix with complex coefficients such that each $\alpha\subseteq <n>$ $A(\alpha)$ has a real eigenvalue such that if $l(\alpha)$ denotes the smallest real eigenvalue of $A(\alpha)$ then $l(\alpha)\leq l(\beta)$ for all $\alpha,\beta$ satisfying $\phi\subset\beta\subseteq \alpha\subseteq <n>$. For all $\alpha\subseteq <n>$ define $F(\alpha)=\det A(\alpha)$  \cite[page 161] {ES}.
If F satisfies the Hadamard-Fischer inequalities on the subsets of $<n>$ then for $0\leq i< k < n$
\begin{par}Assume F is a real valued function that satisfies the Hadamard-Fischer inequalities on the subsets of $<n>$.
We begin by outlining the strategy for proving this result. The proof is in three steps.
\item We first establish the result when k =1 and i=0 for all $n\geq 2$.
\item Next we prove that $E_{k,i}^F \geq U_{k,i}^F$ for the case that $k=n-1$.

We then proceed by induction on n and assume that if $\Omega$ is a set of size n-1  and H is a function satisfying the Hadamard Fisher inequalities on all subsets of $\Omega$ that then $E_{k,i}^{H} \geq U_{k,i}^{H}$ is true for $0\leq i< k<n-1$. For each $x\in <n>$ we define $F^x$ a function on $<n>\backslash\left\{x\right\}$ by $F^x(\alpha)=F(\alpha)$ for all $\alpha\subseteq <n>\backslash\left\{x\right\}$. Then for each $x\in<n>$ $F^x$ satisfies the Hadamard Fisher inequalities on $<n>\backslash\left\{x\right\}$ and hence by our inductive assumption  $E_{k,i}^{F^x} \geq U_{k,i}^{Fx}$ for $1\leq i< k<n-1$.  These inequalities together with the results of step 2 are combined to show that $E_{k,i}^{F} \geq U_{k,i}^{F}$  for $1\leq i< k<n$.
We begin by establishing the result when k=1.
If k=1 then since $0\leq i<k=1$, only i=0 must be considered. Assume k=1 and i = 0.
This establishes the lemma for k=1 and $n\geq 2$.

We now establish step 2.  Let $k>1$, $k=n-1$.  If $\alpha\subseteq <n>$ with $\left|\alpha\right |=k$ and $\beta\subseteq <n>, \alpha\neq\beta,\left|\beta \right|=k$ then $\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|= n-2$. Thus we only have $i=n-2$ to consider.
Thus the lemma  is established for  $ k = n-1$

We now proceed by induction on n and assume that if $\Omega$ is a set of size n-1  and H is any function satisfying the Hadamard Fisher inequalities on all subsets of $\Omega$ then $E_{k,i}^{H} \geq U_{k,i}^{H}$  for $0\leq i< k<n-1$.

$\frac{1}{(n-1)-2(k-i)}\sum_{x=1}^n E_{k,i}^{F^x}$ where for $x\in <n>$ $F^x$ is a Hadamard Function on $<n>\setminus\left\{x\right\}$ where for all $\alpha\subseteq<n>\setminus\left\{x\right\}$ $F^x(\alpha)=F(\alpha)$. By inductive assumption $E_{k,i}^{F^x} \geq U_{k,i}^{F^x}$  for $0\leq i< k<n-1$  Thus $E_{k,i}^{F^x} \geq U_{k,i}^{F^x}$  for $0\leq i< k<n-1$.  $\frac{1}{(n-1)-2(k-i)}\sum_{x=1}^n E_{k,i}^{F_x}\geq\frac{1}{(n-1)-2(k-i)}\sum_{x=1}^n U_{k,i}^{F^x}=$

$(n-1)\sum_{x=1}^n\sum_{\stackrel{k+1=\left|\alpha\subseteq<n>\setminus \left\{x\right\}\right|}{k-1=\left|\beta\subseteq<n>\setminus\left\{x\right\}\right|,\left|\alpha\cap\beta\right|=i}} \frac{F(\alpha)F(\beta)}{(^{n-1}_{2(k-i)})(^{(n-1)-2(k-i)}_i)(^{2(k-i)}_{k-i+1})}=(n-1)U_{k,i}^F$. Thus $E_{k,i}^{F} \geq U_{k,i}^{F}$ for $1\leq i< k <n-1$ and combining this with the proof in step 2 that the inequality holds when $k=n-1$ completes the induction.

The following is established in \cite{IN} for  the case that for all $\alpha\in Q_{ k,<n>}$ $F(\alpha)=\prod_{i\in\alpha}a_i$ where $a_i$  is a non-negative number  for $i\in\alpha$. It is also established  in \cite[Theorem 1]{OH} for the case that for all $\alpha\in Q_{ k,<n>}$ $F(\alpha)= \det M[\alpha]$ where M is an M matrix.
